Z2.strengths: The first screen holds the substance itself: all 13 seats grouped by district, each district with its area and lean, and each seat row named for the person holding or leaving it, with party, status (retiring, incumbent, running for the Senate, not seeking reelection), tags and field mix. A newcomer sees the shape of the whole cycle at once, and the first race's detail sits beside it. The detail pane fits the material: Leaving or Incumbent, District, Seat facts, then a Candidate / Background / Backed by table, with the backers column shown only when a race has backers. Linked races cross-link (Mena's House seat to Conway's Senate seat, Ryu to Salomon). Each race has its own collapsed 'Article text' with the verbatim paragraphs, and the 'No party' versus 'No party preference' and 'Party not stated' distinctions are kept. There is little filler.
Z2.weaknesses: The article's lede (districts that might flip, progressives challenging Democrats from the left) appears only in the 'cycle & source' dialog, so the first screen never says why these races were chosen. 'Mark' is an opaque label, and it only highlights rows: it does not filter them. Creydt's '29-20 majority' sits unflagged against the header's 'Senate 30–19 D'. On a phone the split view gives the list about 40% and the detail about 60% of the height, and the long district prose in the list (5th, 26th) crowds out the seat rows. The full-screen deck and swipe strip are generic machinery that this content does not need.
Z2.regions: Header meta line (majorities, primary, election date); Mark chips (Might flip preselected, Open seat, Own-party challenge); district-grouped race list with seat rows and badges; detail pane (Leaving/Incumbent, District, Seat facts, candidate table with Backed by column); cross-link buttons Mena↔Conway and Ryu↔Salomon; 'Article text for this race' disclosure; Full screen deck; 'cycle & source' dialog; phone split layout after selecting the 42nd.

R9.strengths: It gives the best orientation for a reader who arrives cold: the full headline and lede, a sourced byline, a 'What's at stake' paragraph, House and Senate seat bars (59/39, 30/19) and a four-step calendar. Every race card has a headline that says why it matters ('Rep. Cindy Ryu challenges Sen. Jesse Salomon', 'Open House seat: Rep. Timm Ormsby is retiring'), followed by a summary and the whole field. Nothing is hidden, so find-in-page works. A legend defines each tag in plain words, and 'Could flip' is explicitly tied to what the article says. The filter bar is sticky, with a chamber toggle, an 'N of 12 shown' count and jump-to-district links. It reads naturally as one long page on a phone. The footer flags the article's 30-19 versus 29-20 inconsistency.
R9.weaknesses: No race appears on the first screen at desktop or phone: the races start about 850px down. The page is very long (about 8,900px at desktop and 12,000px on a phone), and apart from the bare district-number jump links there is no compact overview of all the seats. It repeats itself: the district context restates what the race summary or headline says (the Krishnadasan-Valdez 2025 race in the 26th, Ryu challenging Salomon in the 32nd), and some notes are filler ('Also filed to run as a Democrat.', 'Has also filed for the seat.'). A 'Democrat' line also repeats each D chip. Conway's open 29th District Senate seat gets no card of its own, so the Senate filter and 'Open seats 5' leave it out. 'She won that 2025 race' has no antecedent inside its own card.
R9.regions: Hero (headline, lede, source line); What's at stake paragraph and seat bars; calendar strip; races legend; jump-to-district links (tested #d32); sticky filter bar with Could flip + Senate (2 of 12 shown) and chamber toggle; race cards with headline, summary and candidate list; footer note on the Senate split; phone long-scroll layout.

P2.strengths: It is quiet and well organized at the top: the lede, a small table of seats up and Democratic majorities, filter chips with counts (and the 'Might flip' chip explains which seats it covers and why), then district headers carrying area and lean and seat cards with chamber badge, status line, tags and party-count chips. Its fidelity is the best of the four. Each race keeps its verbatim 'Source sentences'. It flags the article's 29-20 versus 30-19 conflict in place, says 'The article names no other candidates for this seat' for Conway's seat, and marks Gary Parker's party as not stated. Cross-reference links (Valdez's seat to the 26th Senate race, Mena to Conway) open and scroll to the related race.
P2.weaknesses: No candidate name is visible until the reader expands a seat ('4 candidates ▾'), and the collapsed content is display:none, so find-in-page cannot reach Danica Noble or Gary Parker. A second layer of toggles then hides one-line facts behind labels such as 'Income tax vote', 'Priorities', 'Platform' and 'Senate math'. That puts the article's pointed contrasts (Hall's vote against Bennett's opposition to the income tax, Warmerdam's platform) two clicks deep. The primary and Election Day dates are pushed to a section at the bottom of the page, not shown up top. Status lines such as 'Rep. David Hackney is running' add little.
P2.regions: Header lede and seats/majority table; filter chips (tested Might flip and its explanatory note); district headers; seat cards with party-count chips and 'N candidates' expanders (opened 32nd Ryu, 26th Valdez, 42nd Senate, 5th Hall on phone); nested candidate toggles ('Earlier work', 'Senate math'); cross-ref link '26th District Senate race →'; 'Source sentences' details; bottom 'The 2026 election' section with calendar.

R5.strengths: The full list of 13 races is visible at once on desktop, with chamber, tags and a chip per candidate, and one click opens a detail pane with labeled facts (Seat, Last race, Area, Lean) and candidate cards that list backers. The header line puts the majorities and both dates on the first screen. The Race filter actually filters, and its counts are correct. Prev/next and the '1 / 13' counter make stepping through races easy. The facts are accurate and closely paraphrased.
R5.weaknesses: A newcomer cannot decode the first screen in ten seconds. The list labels seats by surname alone ('Ormsby', 'Hall', 'Conway'), and the 'Field' column is a string of tiny D/D/D/R letter boxes. The second chip row, 'Mark: Incumbents / Democrats / Republicans / No party', only recolors those letters, which adds a control and little meaning. The lede is missing; the article's framing survives only in the (i) dialog, and 'Might flip' is never defined. Rows are not grouped by district, so the 26th's three races repeat the district each time and the district's context appears only inside each detail card. Candidates sit in boxed cards in a three-column grid, which spreads small facts thinly. On a phone the detail pane is only about 290px tall under the list. The full-screen deck is machinery the content does not need.
R5.regions: Header mono stats line; Race chips (tested Open seat); Mark chips (tested Republicans highlighting); master list (District / Seat / Field chips); detail pane facts list and candidate cards (32nd Ryu, 26th Krishnadasan); prev/next arrows and counter; full-screen deck; (i) election info dialog; phone split after selecting the 42nd.

summary: Z2 won because its first screen is the content itself: a district-grouped list naming who holds or is leaving each seat, with party, status, tags and field mix, beside a detail table that fits the material, and it adds little that is not needed. R9 orients a cold reader best and hides nothing, but it shows no race above the fold and repeats itself down a very long scroll. P2 is the most faithful page but hides every candidate, and even one-line facts, behind expanders. R5 compresses the races into surname labels and letter chips that a newcomer cannot read.
